title: Practice: sampling and bias
intro: Nine questions about planning a fair survey. Several have more than one sensible answer — read the explanations even when you are right.

questions.prompt: Put the four stages of a statistical investigation in order.

items.text: Use the results to answer the question

hints: You cannot collect data until you know what you want to find out.
questions.explanation: Ask → collect → analyse → answer. The answer often suggests a follow-up question, which starts the cycle again.

questions.prompt: Frankie wants to know whether teenagers eat a healthy diet. Match each way of collecting data to its type.

left.text: Asking ten people in the dinner queue what they are buying
Asking the canteen staff for last month's sales list
Looking up canteen food sales figures on the internet
Using his own data sheet to record what his friends eat each lunchtime

hints: Did Frankie collect it himself, or did someone else?
questions.explanation: a and d are primary — Frankie collects them himself. b and c are secondary — somebody else collected them.

options.text: Number of books on a shelf
Type of book (fiction, non-fiction, biography)
Cost of a book
Whether a book is hardback or paperback
Mass of a book

hints: Quantitative means you can measure or count it with a number.
questions.explanation: Number, cost and mass are numerical, so quantitative. Type and cover are descriptions, so qualitative.

questions.prompt: Andreas asks 20 people **outside the swimming pool** whether they like swimming. Why is his sample biased?

options.text: People at a swimming pool are more likely than others to like swimming
20 is an even number
He should have asked only children
It is not biased — everyone was asked the same question

hints: Would people at the shops or the station give the same answers?
questions.explanation: The location means his sample over-represents swimmers. Asking in several places at different times, with a larger sample, would be fairer.

questions.prompt: Beth surveys ten of her friends about healthy eating. Her questions include *"Do you agree that eating too many sweets is bad for you? Yes/No"*. Select **every** reason her results might be biased.

options.text: Ten people is a small sample
Her friends may not represent the whole school
The question is leading — it pushes people towards 'yes'
Yes/No answers give no detail about how much people eat
She used a questionnaire rather than an interview

hints: Think about who she asked, how many, and how the question is worded.
questions.explanation: a–d are all genuine problems. Using a questionnaire is not in itself a source of bias; a well-designed questionnaire is a perfectly good method.

questions.prompt: A larger sample is usually more reliable, but it takes longer and costs more to collect.
hints: Think about both sides: accuracy and effort.
questions.explanation: True. That trade-off is why you have to decide on a sensible sample size, rather than always asking everyone.

questions.prompt: Jamie wants to know what condition people's phones are in after a year. Which question collects **qualitative** data?

options.text: Describe the condition of your phone: as new / a few scratches / lots of scratches / cracked screen
How many scratches are on your phone screen?
How many months have you owned your phone?
How much did your phone cost?

hints: Which answer is a description rather than a number?
questions.explanation: Option a gives descriptions, so it is qualitative. Its advantage is that it captures the overall condition; its disadvantage is that people may judge 'a few scratches' differently. The others are all quantitative.

questions.prompt: In a pilot survey, one person wrote *"half"* for *"How much exercise do you do?"*. What is the best improvement?

options.text: Give tick-box options with units, e.g. 0–1 h, 1–3 h, 3–5 h, 5+ h per week
Remove the question
Only ask people who exercise
Ask the question in capital letters

hints: The problem is that the question does not say what units or time period to use.
questions.explanation: Clear, non-overlapping options with units and a time period mean every answer can be compared. That is exactly what a pilot survey is for — finding questions like this before the real survey.

questions.text: Data you collect yourself is called [[a]] data. Data collected by someone else is [[b]] data. Trying a questionnaire on a few people first is called a [[c]] survey.
hints: The first one comes first — you collect it yourself.
